opus-5.5.text:
That's a question I love, because it's one we often skip over. We tend to assume the agent's world arrives already carved into nice pieces: here's the state, here's the action, here's the reward. In practice, especially when you're building systems that work closely with people, like the prosthetic limbs and assistive devices we work on, someone has to decide what the agent actually gets to sense, how often, and in what form. Those choices quietly shape everything the agent can learn.

My starting point is to keep the units as close to the raw stream of experience as I reasonably can. An agent lives in a continuous flow of sensation and action through time. If I, as the designer, pre-digest that stream into high-level features I think matter, I'm baking in my assumptions about the problem. Sometimes that's fine, but often the most interesting structure is the stuff I didn't anticipate. So I'd rather give the agent a rich, fairly low-level sensorimotor stream and let it build its own abstractions.

The second piece is time. Choosing the timestep is choosing a unit of experience. If it's too coarse, you miss the dynamics that matter, like the fine timing of a muscle signal when someone's trying to open a hand. If it's too fine, credit assignment gets harder and computation goes up. So the temporal grain should match the timescale of the interaction you care about, and ideally the agent can reason across several timescales at once.

Third, I like to think of prediction as the glue. A powerful idea from our group and the broader Alberta tradition is that knowledge can be expressed as predictions about future signals, things like general value functions. Once you frame it that way, the fundamental units become the signals the agent can predict and the actions that affect them. A good unit of experience is one that supports useful predictions. If a signal is unpredictable noise, or so redundant it adds nothing, it isn't pulling its weight.

Finally, when there's a person in the loop, the person is part of the agent's experience too. Their signals, their corrections, even their hesitation are data. So I try not to draw a hard line between "the environment" and "the user." In a prosthetic, the human and the machine are learning about each other at the same time, and the units of experience need to support that two-way relationship.

So in short: stay close to the raw stream, pick a time grain that fits the interaction, judge units by how well they support prediction, and remember that the human is part of the world the agent is learning about.

r002.rationale: It says knowledge can be expressed as predictions about future signals and identifies predictable signals as fundamental units of experience.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a question I come back to constantly, because it sits underneath everything else we do. The way I think about it, the fundamental unit of an agent's experience is the moment: the agent gets an observation from the world, it takes an action, it gets a reward signal, and that cycle repeats. Observation, action, reward. That's the atom. Everything else, all the representations, all the predictions, all the knowledge the agent builds up, gets constructed out of that stream of moments.

Now, where it gets interesting is deciding what counts as an observation and what counts as an action, because those choices aren't handed to us by nature. If you're building a prosthetic arm, which is a lot of the work my group has done, you have to ask: is the observation the raw electrical signal off the muscle, sampled thousands of times a second? Or is it some smoothed, windowed feature? Is the action a tiny increment of motor torque, or is it "close the hand"? Every one of those decisions bakes in assumptions about the timescale at which the agent lives.

My bias is to push those choices as close to the raw sensorimotor stream as we can, and to keep the time step short. The reason is that if I do the abstraction for the agent, I'm smuggling in my own understanding of the problem, and I'm probably wrong about some of it. If instead the agent experiences the world at a fine temporal grain, it has the chance to discover the regularities itself, to build its own predictions about what its sensors will say next and how its actions change that. We've seen this with our temporal-difference learning work: the agent can learn thousands of these little predictions about its own experience, and those predictions become the vocabulary it uses to understand the world. That vocabulary emerges from the stream rather than being dictated by the designer.

The counterargument, which I take seriously, is that short time steps and raw signals make learning harder and slower, and in a clinical setting you don't have infinite time with a person. So in practice we often end up with a hybrid, where we give the agent a reasonable starting point but preserve its ability to learn and revise. But philosophically, I want the experience to be the agent's own. The moment, as it actually unfolds in the agent's sensors and motors, is the honest starting point. Everything above that should be earned.

r001.rationale: The response describes observation, action, and reward cycles and mentions learned predictions, but does not explain that generalized value functions extend value prediction from reward to any signal of interest.

r002.rationale: It says moments are the fundamental unit and that learned predictions become a vocabulary for understanding the world. It does not clearly identify predictions of future signals as the foundational units of experience.

astra-6.text:
I think the key question is: what distinctions does the agent need to make to interact effectively with its world? We often start with units that make sense to us—objects, words, categories—but those may not be the most useful starting point for the agent.

I tend to think in terms of predictions grounded in the agent’s own experience. Given what I’m sensing, and given how I might act, what do I expect to happen next? That could be something very immediate, like whether a movement will produce contact, or something that unfolds over a longer period, like how much effort it will take to accomplish a task.

What’s appealing about that is that the agent can check those predictions against what actually happens. They have meaning through interaction. And you can build richer representations out of them, across different timescales.

So I wouldn’t necessarily look for one fixed, universal set of units. I’d ask whether the units we choose let the agent learn from experience, anticipate the consequences of its actions, and improve the way it participates in the world.

r001.rationale: The response discusses predictions from experience but does not explain generalized value functions or extending value prediction from future reward to any signal of interest.

r002.rationale: It frames predictions of what will happen next, grounded in the agent’s sensing and actions, as a way to define useful units of the agent’s experience.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the starting point is the interaction between the agent and its world. What can it sense, what can it change through its actions, and what consequences matter to it? Those choices give you a grounding for experience.

But I wouldn’t assume that the units we choose as designers are necessarily the units the agent should use forever. A sensor reading or a motor command is one level of description. Through learning, an agent can build predictions that bring those signals together over time: if I act in this way, what will happen next? Those predictions can themselves become useful building blocks for further learning.

So I think about this as an ongoing process of constructing useful abstractions. The question is whether a particular unit helps the agent predict, make decisions, and achieve its goals through interaction.

r001.rationale: The response discusses predictions of what happens after actions, but does not explain generalized value functions or extending value prediction from reward to any signal of interest.

r002.rationale: It calls learned predictions useful building blocks for further learning, but does not clearly propose predictions of future signals as the foundational units of the agent’s experience.
